# Walther Dobbertin: Visualizing German East Africa – A Comprehensive Biographical and Historical Analysis
## 1\. Introduction
### 1.1. The Photographer as Historian and Mythmaker
In the annals of German colonial history, few figures occupy as complex and visually significant a position as Walther Dobbertin (1882–1961). A photographer, publisher, and fervent colonial revisionist, Dobbertin was not merely a passive observer of the German imperial project in East Africa (*Deutsch-Ostafrika*); he was one of its primary visual architects. Operating during the zenith of the Wilhelmine empire’s overseas expansion and continuing his influence through the tumultuous years of the Weimar Republic and the Third Reich, Dobbertin produced an archive that remains the definitive visual record of German Tanzania.

His oeuvre, comprising thousands of glass-plate negatives, prints, and postcards, transcends the genre of commercial photography. It serves as a comprehensive inventory of the colonial mindset, documenting the infrastructural ambitions, racial hierarchies, and environmental transformations that characterized German rule from 1903 to 1918\. Furthermore, his unique status as the sole photographer to document the German side of the East African Campaign during World War I grants his work an unparalleled historical weight. Through his lens, the guerrilla warfare of General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck was immortalized, and the figure of the *Askari* (African soldier) was elevated into a symbol of loyalty that would later be weaponized by revanchist propaganda.

However, a biographical study of Dobbertin cannot be limited to his years in Africa. His trajectory from a studio owner in Dar es Salaam to a bookseller in the Harz Mountains, and subsequently to a functionary in the Nazi paramilitary apparatus (*Sturmabteilung* or SA), offers a microcosm of the German colonial consciousness itself. It reveals how the "loss" of the colonies in 1919 was processed, mythologized, and integrated into the nationalist fervor that fueled the rise of National Socialism.

In the contemporary era, Dobbertin’s legacy has undergone a profound re-evaluation. No longer viewed simply as neutral historical documentation, his images are scrutinized by post-colonial scholars for their role in constructing the "colonial gaze"—a visual paradigm that codified the domination of the European settler over the African landscape and body. Simultaneously, environmental historians have rediscovered his high-resolution landscape photography, utilizing his century-old images of the Usambara Mountains to map long-term ecological changes, deforestation, and land-use patterns. Thus, Dobbertin remains a vital, if controversial, interlocutor in the ongoing dialogue between Europe and Africa, his work serving as both a testament to imperial hubris and an unintended baseline for ecological science.

### 1.2. Scope of the Report
This report provides an exhaustive analysis of Walther Dobbertin’s life, work, and legacy. It draws upon fragmentary archival records, contemporary academic re-assessments, and the visual evidence of the photographs themselves. The narrative is structured chronologically but pauses frequently to engage in deep thematic analysis of the subjects Dobbertin captured—from the mechanics of the *Schutztruppe* to the botany of the Usambara rainforests. It also addresses the controversies surrounding the dating of his wartime images and the specific mechanisms of his post-war propaganda work.

## 2\. Early Life and the Imperial Context (1882–1903)
### 2.1. Berlin in the Wilhelmine Era
Walther Dobbertin was born on August 28, 1882, in Berlin, the beating heart of the newly unified German Empire (*Deutsches Reich*) . His birth coincided with a pivotal moment in German history. Under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, and later Kaiser Wilhelm II, Berlin was transforming into a global metropolis, characterized by rapid industrialization, explosive population growth, and a burgeoning sense of national destiny.

The 1880s were the decade of Germany’s "scramble for Africa." Just two years after Dobbertin’s birth, the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 formalized the partition of the African continent, granting Germany control over vast territories in South West Africa, Cameroon, Togo, and East Africa. Growing up in this atmosphere, young Dobbertin would have been surrounded by the propaganda of empire: colonial exhibitions, ethnographic shows (*Völkerschauen*), and the adventure literature that romanticized life in the tropics. The colonial project was presented not merely as an economic necessity but as a national duty, a sentiment that would profoundly shape Dobbertin’s worldview.

### 2.2. Training and Artistic Foundations
Coming from a family of craftsmen, Dobbertin likely inherited a respect for technical precision and manual skill . His ancestral roots in Mecklenburg—specifically the region near the historic Dobbertin Abbey—suggest a background steeped in the traditions of Northern Germany .

For his professional education, Dobbertin moved to Rostock, a Hanseatic port city on the Baltic Sea . Here, he completed an apprenticeship as a photographer. Photography in the turn of the 20th century was a demanding trade requiring knowledge of chemistry, optics, and lighting. The transition from wet-plate to dry-plate processes was well underway, making photography more mobile, yet it remained a cumbersome endeavor involving heavy glass plates and large-format cameras.

Crucially, Dobbertin supplemented his technical training with painting courses . This artistic education is evident in his later work. His landscapes are rarely mere snapshots; they are composed with a painterly eye for balance, perspective, and the "sublime." He understood the rules of the Golden Ratio and the use of foreground interest to lead the viewer’s eye into the distance—techniques he would apply to the dramatic topography of the East African rift valley. This fusion of the technician and the artist would become his hallmark, allowing him to produce images that were commercially viable as postcards yet aesthetically sophisticated enough to endure as art.

## 3\. Arrival in "The Place of Peace": Early Years in Dar es Salaam (1903–1906)
### 3.1. The Voyage and Arrival
In 1903, at the age of 21, Dobbertin joined the steady stream of Germans emigrating to *Deutsch-Ostafrika*.3 The journey itself, typically undertaken via the Suez Canal on steamers of the German East Africa Line (*Deutsche Ost-Afrika Linie*), was a rite of passage for colonial settlers.

He arrived in Dar es Salaam ("Haven of Peace"), the administrative capital of the colony. In 1903, Dar es Salaam was a city in transition. Established by the Sultan of Zanzibar in the 1860s and taken over by the Germans in the 1890s, it was being rebuilt to reflect German order. Wide, tree-lined avenues, stone administrative buildings (*Bomas*), and a botanical garden were under construction, designed to project permanence and authority. However, the colony was still reeling from the aftershocks of the Maji Maji Rebellion (1905–1907), a brutal conflict that would result in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Africans. Dobbertin arrived in the quiet before this storm, or perhaps during its early rumbles, entering a society that was strictly stratified by race and class.

### 3.2. The Vincenti Interlude and Legal Disputes
Dobbertin did not immediately establish his own studio. The photographic market in Dar es Salaam was small and dominated by a few established names, most notably Carl Vincenti . Vincenti documented the social life of the colonial elite and the maritime activities of the harbor. Dobbertin secured employment as an assistant in Vincenti’s studio, a position that would have introduced him to the specific challenges of tropical photography .

Working in the tropics presented unique difficulties. High humidity could cause fungal growth on lenses and ruin photographic emulsions. The intense equatorial sun created harsh contrasts that required careful exposure management. Developing chemicals deteriorated rapidly in the heat. Under Vincenti, Dobbertin would have mastered the logistical supply chains necessary to import glass plates and chemicals from Germany, a knowledge base that would later prove crucial for his own business.

The relationship between the master and the apprentice ended in acrimony. Sometime between 1903 and 1906, Vincenti took Dobbertin to court, accusing him of the theft of photographic materials . While the specific court records are not detailed in the snippets, the incident suggests a bitter rivalry and perhaps Dobbertin’s ambition outgrowing his subordinate role. The rupture was decisive; Dobbertin left Vincenti’s employ and, rather than returning to Germany in disgrace, chose to compete.

## 4\. The Dobbertin Studio: Visualizing the Colony (1906–1914)
### 4.1. Establishing a Commercial Empire
In 1906, Dobbertin opened his own independent studio in Dar es Salaam . The timing was fortuitous. The suppression of the Maji Maji Rebellion marked the beginning of a period of intense economic development known as "scientific colonialism" under Governor Albrecht von Rechenberg. There was a demand for images that showed the colony not as a war zone, but as a site of progress, investment, and "civilization."

Dobbertin proved to be an astute businessman. He expanded his operations beyond the capital, establishing branches or retail presence in Tanga, the colony’s second port and the center of the sisal industry, and Moshi, the gateway to the coffee plantations of Kilimanjaro . His studio stamp—*Walther Dobbertin Daressalam*—became a seal of quality . He sold prints, framed portraits, and crucially, postcards. In an era before mass media, the postcard was the primary means by which the visual reality of the empire was disseminated to the metropole. Every German settler sending a postcard home was, in effect, a propagandist for the colony, and Dobbertin provided the imagery.

### 4.2. Themes of the Pre-War Archive
Dobbertin’s pre-war work can be categorized into three distinct but overlapping genres: the documentation of infrastructure ("German Work"), ethnographic typology ("The Native"), and the romantic landscape ("The German Tropics").

#### 4.2.1. Infrastructure and "German Work"
A central theme of Dobbertin’s work was the transformation of the African landscape through German engineering. He obsessively documented the construction of the Central Railway (*Mittellandbahn*) which began in Dar es Salaam in 1905 and reached Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika in 1914\. His camera captured the laying of tracks, the construction of steel bridges over ravines, and the steam locomotives that symbolized industrial modernity .

These images were celebrated in his 1920 publication *Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika* (Of German Work in German East Africa) . The title is instructive: it frames the colony not as a land of natural resources, but as a canvas for *German* labor and ingenuity. One iconic image from this series shows a sisal plantation . Rows of Agave sisalana stretch to the horizon, a geometry of order imposed on the chaotic bush. African laborers are present—cutting and bundling leaves—but they are depicted as anonymous components of the production machine, their individuality subsumed by the industrial scale of the enterprise. This visual erasure of the African subject's humanity in favor of their labor power was a hallmark of colonial photography.

#### 4.2.2. The Ethnographic Lens and the "Colonial Gaze"
Dobbertin also produced a vast array of images depicting the indigenous peoples of East Africa. These photographs catered to the European fascination with the "exotic." He produced studio portraits of Maasai warriors, Swahili women, and various "tribal types," often staged with traditional artifacts to emphasize their "otherness" .

Post-colonial scholars characterize this as the "colonial gaze." The subjects were often posed passively, to be looked at, categorized, and possessed by the European viewer. However, Dobbertin’s work also contains slippages that reveal the agency of the colonized.

The Case of "Mr. Barnabas": 
One particularly significant photograph, analyzed by historian G. Krautwald, depicts a man identified as "Mr. Barnabas" . Barnabas, a Makua man educated at a government school in Lindi, is shown seated, reading a copy of the Swahili-language newspaper Kiongozi to a group of five fellow soldiers and porters . Taken during the war (or shortly before), this image is complex. On one level, it is propaganda: it showcases the success of the German educational mission and the loyalty of the Askari. The composition is choreographed, with Barnabas at the center, radiating knowledge. Yet, it also documents the reality of African literacy and the formation of a new social class—the Askari intelligentsia—who would play a crucial role in the colony’s future. The photograph demonstrates that the newspaper was not just a tool of German power, but a medium through which Africans were negotiating their own modernity.

#### 4.2.3. The Usambara Landscapes
Perhaps Dobbertin’s most enduring contribution is his landscape photography of the Usambara Mountains. This range, with its cool climate and lush rainforests, was the center of European settlement. Dobbertin traveled extensively here, hauling his heavy camera gear up steep trails to capture panoramic vistas of the Lua Valley, the mission station at Gare, and the precipitous drops of the escarpment .

These images are technically superb. The glass plates captured an immense amount of detail, from the species of trees in the forest canopy to the erosion patterns on the cultivated slopes. Aesthetically, they framed the Usambaras as a "German Heimat" in Africa—a landscape that, with its orderly fields and misty peaks, could remind a settler of the Black Forest or the Harz.

### 4.3. Technology and Method
Dobbertin operated in an era of transition for photographic technology. He primarily used large-format cameras with glass plates (likely dry gelatin plates). These plates, often 13x18cm or larger, offered resolution that rivals modern high-end digital cameras . However, they were heavy, fragile, and slow.

To achieve his shots, Dobbertin was as much an expedition leader as a photographer. He required porters to carry his equipment, tripods, and darkroom supplies. In the field, he had to judge exposure by eye, as light meters were primitive. The distinct aesthetic of his photos—deep depth of field, sharp focus throughout—was a result of using small apertures (high f-stop), which in turn required long exposure times. This necessitated the absolute stillness of his subjects, contributing to the stiff, posed look of his portraits, while his landscapes benefited from the clarity.

## 5\. The War Years: The Only Eye of the Schutztruppe (1914–1916)
### 5.1. Mobilization and the Schutztruppe
When World War I erupted in August 1914, German East Africa found itself surrounded by hostile colonial powers: British Kenya to the north, the Belgian Congo to the west, and Portuguese Mozambique to the south. The commander of the *Schutztruppe*, Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, adopted a strategy of aggressive defense, aiming to tie down as many Allied troops as possible in a protracted guerrilla war.

Upon mobilization, the German male population was conscripted. Dobbertin joined the *Schutztruppe*, not merely as a soldier but in a capacity that utilized his professional skills . While the Western Front had official propaganda companies (*Bild- und Filmamt*), the East African theater was isolated. Dobbertin became, by default and by talent, the primary—and arguably the only—photographer systematically documenting the German campaign .

### 5.2. Documenting the Campaign
Dobbertin’s wartime archive is a unique historical document. It captures the transformation of the colonial police force into a battle-hardened army.

The Battle of Tanga and the Königsberg: 
He documented the aftermath of the Battle of Tanga (November 1914), a decisive German victory against a poorly led British amphibious landing. More significantly, he chronicled the logistical miracle of the SMS Königsberg. After the German cruiser was trapped and sunk in the Rufiji Delta, its ten 10.5cm naval guns were salvaged. Dobbertin photographed these massive weapons being mounted on improvised gun carriages and dragged through the bush by teams of hundreds of porters . These images serve as a testament to the ingenuity and improvisation that characterized the German war effort. 
The Askari and the "Loyalty" Myth: 
His most politically potent images from this period are those of the Askari. He photographed them on the march, cleaning their Mauser rifles, and manning machine gun nests. These photos emphasize discipline, order, and an apparent camaraderie between white officers and black soldiers . 
One famous series shows "Camel-mounted Schutztruppe" on patrol near the Kilimanjaro/Longido area, illustrating the diverse and adaptive nature of the force . Another depicts a machine gun team in action, the tension of combat frozen on the glass plate . These images would later be stripped of their context and used to propagate the myth that the Askari fought out of sheer devotion to the Kaiser, ignoring the complex motivations of pay, status, and coercion that actually drove recruitment.

### 5.3. Lost Film and Cinematic Ambitions
Snippet 1 mentions a fascinating detail: Dobbertin also shot scenes for a documentary film during the early stages of the war. Cinema was in its infancy, and a war documentary from Africa would have been a sensation. Tragically, this footage has been lost to history, likely destroyed during the retreat or confiscated. We are left only with his still images to reconstruct the visual narrative he intended to create.

## 6\. Captivity and the Mystery of the "Lost Years" (1916–1920)
### 6.1. Capture and Imprisonment
By 1916, the sheer numerical superiority of the Allied forces (British, South African, Indian, Belgian) began to tell. The *Schutztruppe* was forced to abandon the Northern Railway and retreat south into the Rufiji wilderness. It was during this period of retreat that Dobbertin was captured by the British .

He spent the remainder of the war—roughly 1916 to 1919—as a Prisoner of War (POW). The conditions of his imprisonment are not detailed in the snippets, but German POWs in East Africa were typically held in camps in Egypt, India, or localized holding areas in Dar es Salaam before repatriation.

### 6.2. The 1918 Photo Controversy
A significant historical puzzle arises regarding photographs in the Dobbertin archive dated to 1918 and early 1919\. Snippet 4 highlights a specific image showing General von Lettow-Vorbeck and a British staff officer, dated March 1918 (or possibly post-surrender in 1919). 
If Dobbertin was a prisoner in 1916, how could he have taken a photo of Lettow-Vorbeck in the field in 1918? 
Several theories exist:

1. **Attribution Error:** The photo was taken by a British photographer or another German soldier and later acquired by Dobbertin, who added it to his collection. 
2. **Post-Surrender Photography:** Following the Armistice in November 1918, Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered at Abercorn and marched his troops to Dar es Salaam. It is possible that Dobbertin, if held in Dar es Salaam, was released or allowed to photograph the arrival of the undefeated General in early 1919 before their mutual repatriation. 
3. **Dating Error:** The dates in the archives may simply be incorrect.

The consensus among historians tends toward attribution error or the acquisition of negatives from other sources. The Bundesarchiv collection, "Nachlass Walther Dobbertin," contains materials he *owned*, not necessarily only those he *took*, though he is the primary author of the vast majority.

### 6.3. Alwine Dobbertin and the Rescue of the Archive
While Walther languished in a POW camp, his wife, Alwine Dobbertin, performed a feat of archival rescue. As the British administration took over and German property was seized, she managed to smuggle the heavy, fragile glass plates out of the country . 
The logistics of this are remarkable. Glass plates are dense and breakable. Smuggling hundreds of them past military censors and onto a repatriation ship suggests a high degree of determination and perhaps the assistance of sympathetic officials or hidden compartments. Without Alwine’s actions, the visual history of German East Africa would be significantly poorer, and Walther’s post-war career would have been impossible.

## 7\. Weimar Revisionism: The Archive as Propaganda (1920–1933)
### 7.1. Return to the Heimat
In 1920, the Dobbertins were repatriated to Germany. They arrived in a country that had changed unrecognizable: the Kaiser had abdicated, the economy was in ruins, and the Treaty of Versailles had stripped Germany of all its colonies. 
Dobbertin settled in Northern Germany, in the quiet heathland south of Hamburg. He moved to Wiedenhof, a district of Jesteburg, and established a business in the nearby towns of Buchholz and Harburg . 
He opened a bookshop (*Buchhandlung*) and a publishing house (*Kunstverlag*). His primary asset was the crates of glass plates Alwine had saved. In a Germany humiliated by defeat, there was a potent market for nostalgia—for images of a time when Germany was a world power with a tropical empire.

### 7.2. "The Colonial Lie" and Revisionist Publishing
The Weimar Republic was rife with "colonial revisionism." This political movement sought to refute the "Colonial Guilt Lie" (Kolonialschuldlüge)—the Allied justification that Germany was too brutal to rule colonies. Revisionists argued that German rule had been benevolent, scientific, and progressive. 
Dobbertin’s photos were the perfect evidence for this argument. He began publishing postcards and books that emphasized "German Work." His 1920 book Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika was an explicit visual rebuttal to Versailles. It showed bridges, schools, and hospitals, arguing visually that Germany had developed the territory for the benefit of all .

### 7.3. *Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers* (1932)
The culmination of this revisionist phase was the publication of Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks (Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers) in 1932.1 Self-published from his home in Wiedenhof, this book contained 120 high-quality copperplate engravings of his wartime photos. 
The book was not just a history; it was a hagiography. It presented the East African campaign as a clean, heroic struggle, contrasting sharply with the industrialized slaughter of the Western Front. The captions, written in a nationalist register, celebrated the "fidelity" of the Askari and the genius of Lettow-Vorbeck. 
This book was instrumental in solidifying the legend of Lettow-Vorbeck, who was himself a prominent right-wing political figure in the Weimar era. Dobbertin’s images provided the visual iconography for the General’s memoirs, creating a feedback loop of myth-making that portrayed the colonial army as "undefeated in the field" .

## 8\. The Third Reich: Photography in the Service of the State (1933–1945)
### 8.1. Aligning with the Regime
When the Nazis seized power in 1933, the colonial revisionist movement was absorbed into the state’s expansionist ideology. Dobbertin, already a nationalist and a veteran, aligned himself with the new order. 
He joined the Sturmabteilung (SA), the "Brownshirts," which was the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party . Membership in the SA indicates that Dobbertin was not merely a passive fellow traveler but an active participant in the party apparatus. 
Furthermore, he became a district leader (Kreisleiter or similar local functionary) for the Reichskolonialbund (RKB), the Reich Colonial League . The RKB, led by Franz Ritter von Epp, was tasked with keeping the "colonial thought" alive in the German population, preparing them for the eventual reclamation of the overseas territories.

### 8.2. The Use of the Archive in Nazi Propaganda
Under the aegis of the RKB, Dobbertin’s archive was mobilized for mass propaganda. His photos were converted into lantern slides for lectures given in schools and community halls across Germany. They were used in major colonial exhibitions, such as the ones in Dresden (1939) and Vienna (1940) . 
In the Nazi context, Dobbertin’s images of orderly plantations and loyal African subordinates took on a darker ideological hue. They were used to validate the Nazi theories of racial hierarchy and the concept of Lebensraum (living space). The "German Work" in Africa was presented as a precursor to the German colonization of Eastern Europe—a demonstration of the German ability to order and exploit "primitive" lands. 
Dobbertin continued to profit from this. In 1933, his photos illustrated Alfred Funke’s novel Schwarz-Weiß-Rot über Ostafrika, a piece of colonial fiction that indoctrinated the youth with the romance of the lost empire .

## 9\. Denazification and the Quiet End (1945–1961)
### 9.1. The Fall and Rehabilitation
With the collapse of the Third Reich in 1945, the colonial dream was finally extinguished. British troops occupied Northern Germany. Dobbertin, as a known member of the SA and a Nazi functionary, fell under the scrutiny of the denazification process. 
The British authorities revoked his business license in 1945, effectively banning him from publishing or selling books . This was a standard measure against those deemed to have actively supported the regime. 
However, like many of his generation, Dobbertin was eventually rehabilitated. The exact date of the restoration of his license is unclear, but by the late 1940s or early 1950s, he was back in business .

### 9.2. The Final Years
He spent the 1950s running his bookshop in Wiedenhof. The clamor for colonies had died down, replaced by the Cold War and the distinct challenges of the Wirtschaftswunder. Dobbertin remained a local figure, the keeper of a specific, fading memory. 
Remarkably, he never returned to Africa during the interwar or Nazi periods. It was only in 1960/1961 that he planned a return trip to Tanzania, which was then on the verge of independence from British rule. He intended to revisit the landscapes he had photographed half a century earlier. 
Fate intervened. Walther Dobbertin died on January 12, 1961, in Jesteburg-Wiedenhof, shortly before his scheduled departure . He was 78 years old.

## 10\. The Afterlife of the Archive: Scientific and Historical Legacy
### 10.1. The Bundesarchiv Acquisition
Following his death, his widow sold the collection to the German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) in Koblenz. The "Nachlass Walther Dobbertin" (BILD 105\) comprises approximately 3,000 images . This acquisition transformed the collection from a private commercial asset into public property, accessible to researchers. 
The archive includes not just East Africa, but also images from German South West Africa (Namibia) and Cameroon, though East Africa remains the core .

### 10.2. The Usambara Knowledge Project: Science from History
In recent years, the most innovative use of Dobbertin’s work has come from the field of environmental history. Professor Chris Conte of Utah State University initiated the *Usambara Knowledge Project*, which uses Dobbertin’s landscapes as scientific data points .

Methodology of Re-photography: 
Conte and his team located the exact spots where Dobbertin stood in roughly 1910\. They took new photographs to create a "then and now" comparison. 
The findings were revelatory:

* **Forest Cover:** Contrary to narratives of pure destruction, some areas showed forest regeneration, while others showed the replacement of indigenous cloud forest with exotic species introduced by the Germans (eucalyptus, wattle). 
* **Land Use:** The photos revealed the transition from the German plantation economy to the peasant agriculture of modern Tanzania. 
* **Demography:** The expansion of settlements into previously uninhabited slopes was visibly measurable.

Dobbertin’s technical obsession with sharpness and depth of field meant that individual trees and erosion gullies from 1910 could be identified, making his "colonial gaze" an inadvertent tool for modern conservation science .

### 10.3. Post-Colonial Critique
Scholars like Heike I. Schmidt and others have used the archive to critique the visual culture of colonialism. They argue that Dobbertin’s photos did not just record reality; they created it. By photographing the "native" in specific ways—as a servant, a warrior, or a type—Dobbertin helped to construct the racial categories that underpinned colonial rule. 
However, the archive is also seen as a site of "visual repatriation." Digitalization projects are increasingly making these images available to Tanzanians, allowing descendants of the Askari and the porters to see their ancestors, not as colonial subjects, but as historical actors in their own right.

## 11\. Conclusion
Walther Dobbertin was a man of his time, and his life followed the tragic arc of German nationalism in the 20th century. He was a pioneer who helped build a colony, a soldier who fought to defend it, a propagandist who tried to resurrect it, and finally, a relic of a vanished world. 
His intentions were undoubtedly colonialist; he sought to glorify "German Work" and German dominance. Yet, the quality and comprehensiveness of his work have allowed it to escape his ideological grasp. Today, his photographs serve purposes he could never have imagined: they are evidence for the prosecution in the court of history regarding colonial exploitation, but they are also precious baselines for the ecological salvation of the Usambara Mountains. In the end, Dobbertin left behind more than just propaganda; he left a high-resolution memory of a world that changed the course of African and European history forever.

The colonial project was presented not merely as an economic necessity but as a national duty, a sentiment that would profoundly shape Dobbertin’s worldview.
Walther Dobbertin likely inherited a respect for technical precision and manual skill, coming from a family of craftsmen.
Walther Dobbertin's ancestral roots in Mecklenburg, specifically the region near the historic Dobbertin Abbey, suggest a background steeped in the traditions of Northern Germany.
For his professional education, Walther Dobbertin moved to Rostock, a Hanseatic port city on the Baltic Sea.
Walther Dobbertin completed an apprenticeship as a photographer in Rostock.
Photography in the turn of the 20th century was a demanding trade requiring knowledge of chemistry, optics, and lighting.

The transition from wet-plate to dry-plate processes was well underway in photography, making it more mobile, yet it remained a cumbersome endeavor involving heavy glass plates and large-format cameras.
Walther Dobbertin supplemented his technical training with painting courses.
Walther Dobbertin's artistic education is evident in his later work.
Walther Dobbertin's landscapes are rarely mere snapshots; they are composed with a painterly eye for balance, perspective, and the "sublime."

Walther Dobbertin understood the rules of the Golden Ratio and the use of foreground interest to lead the viewer’s eye into the distance, techniques he would apply to the dramatic topography of the East African rift valley.

The fusion of the technician and the artist became Walther Dobbertin's hallmark, allowing him to produce images that were commercially viable as postcards yet aesthetically sophisticated enough to endure as art.
In 1903, at the age of 21, Walther Dobbertin joined the steady stream of Germans emigrating to Deutsch-Ostafrika.
The journey to Deutsch-Ostafrika was typically undertaken via the Suez Canal on steamers of the German East Africa Line (Deutsche Ost-Afrika Linie).
Walther Dobbertin arrived in Dar es Salaam ("Haven of Peace"), the administrative capital of the colony.
In 1903, Dar es Salaam was a city in transition.
Dar es Salaam was established by the Sultan of Zanzibar in the 1860s and taken over by the Germans in the 1890s.

Dar es Salaam was being rebuilt to reflect German order, with wide, tree-lined avenues, stone administrative buildings (Bomas), and a botanical garden under construction, designed to project permanence and authority.
The colony was still reeling from the aftershocks of the Maji Maji Rebellion (1905–1907), a brutal conflict that would result in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Africans.
Walther Dobbertin arrived in the quiet before the storm of the Maji Maji Rebellion, or perhaps during its early rumbles, entering a society that was strictly stratified by race and class.
Walther Dobbertin did not immediately establish his own studio upon arrival in Dar es Salaam.
The photographic market in Dar es Salaam was small and dominated by a few established names, most notably Carl Vincenti.
Carl Vincenti documented the social life of the colonial elite and the maritime activities of the harbor in Dar es Salaam.
Walther Dobbertin secured employment as an assistant in Carl Vincenti’s studio, a position that would have introduced him to the specific challenges of tropical photography.
Working in the tropics presented unique difficulties for photography, such as high humidity causing fungal growth on lenses and ruining photographic emulsions.
The intense equatorial sun created harsh contrasts that required careful exposure management in tropical photography.
Developing chemicals deteriorated rapidly in the heat of the tropics.
Under Carl Vincenti, Walther Dobbertin would have mastered the logistical supply chains necessary to import glass plates and chemicals from Germany.
The relationship between Carl Vincenti and Walther Dobbertin ended in acrimony.
Sometime between 1903 and 1906, Carl Vincenti took Walther Dobbertin to court, accusing him of the theft of photographic materials.
The incident where Carl Vincenti took Walther Dobbertin to court suggests a bitter rivalry and perhaps Dobbertin’s ambition outgrowing his subordinate role.
Walther Dobbertin left Carl Vincenti’s employ and chose to compete, rather than returning to Germany in disgrace.
In 1906, Walther Dobbertin opened his own independent studio in Dar es Salaam.

The timing of Walther Dobbertin opening his studio was fortuitous, as the suppression of the Maji Maji Rebellion marked the beginning of a period of intense economic development known as "scientific colonialism" under Governor Albrecht von Rechenberg.
There was a demand for images that showed the colony not as a war zone, but as a site of progress, investment, and "civilization."
Walther Dobbertin proved to be an astute businessman.
Walther Dobbertin expanded his operations beyond Dar es Salaam, establishing branches or retail presence in Tanga and Moshi.
Walther Dobbertin’s studio stamp, "Walther Dobbertin Daressalam", became a seal of quality.
Walther Dobbertin sold prints, framed portraits, and postcards.
In an era before mass media, the postcard was the primary means by which the visual reality of the empire was disseminated to the metropole.
Every German settler sending a postcard home was, in effect, a propagandist for the colony, and Walther Dobbertin provided the imagery.

Walther Dobbertin’s pre-war work can be categorized into three distinct but overlapping genres: the documentation of infrastructure ("German Work"), ethnographic typology ("The Native"), and the romantic landscape ("The German Tropics").
A central theme of Walther Dobbertin’s work was the transformation of the African landscape through German engineering.
Walther Dobbertin obsessively documented the construction of the Central Railway (Mittellandbahn), which began in Dar es Salaam in 1905 and reached Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika in 1914.
Walther Dobbertin’s camera captured the laying of tracks, the construction of steel bridges over ravines, and the steam locomotives that symbolized industrial modernity.
Walther Dobbertin’s images were celebrated in his 1920 publication Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika (Of German Work in German East Africa).
The title of Walther Dobbertin's 1920 publication, Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika, frames the colony not as a land of natural resources, but as a canvas for German labor and ingenuity.
One iconic image from Walther Dobbertin's series on infrastructure and "German Work" shows a sisal plantation.
Rows of Agave sisalana stretch to the horizon in Walther Dobbertin's image of a sisal plantation, representing a geometry of order imposed on the chaotic bush.

African laborers are present in Walther Dobbertin's sisal plantation image, cutting and bundling leaves, but they are depicted as anonymous components of the production machine, their individuality subsumed by the industrial scale of the enterprise.
The visual erasure of the African subject's humanity in favor of their labor power was a hallmark of colonial photography.
Walther Dobbertin also produced a vast array of images depicting the indigenous peoples of East Africa.
Walther Dobbertin's photographs of indigenous peoples catered to the European fascination with the "exotic."
Walther Dobbertin produced studio portraits of Maasai warriors, Swahili women, and various "tribal types," often staged with traditional artifacts to emphasize their "otherness."
Post-colonial scholars characterize Walther Dobbertin's ethnographic photography as the "colonial gaze."
The subjects in Walther Dobbertin's ethnographic photographs were often posed passively, to be looked at, categorized, and possessed by the European viewer.
Walther Dobbertin’s work also contains slippages that reveal the agency of the colonized.
One particularly significant photograph, analyzed by historian G. Krautwald, depicts a man identified as "Mr. Barnabas."

Barnabas, a Makua man educated at a government school in Lindi, is shown seated, reading a copy of the Swahili-language newspaper Kiongozi to a group of five fellow soldiers and porters in a photograph by Walther Dobbertin.
The image of Mr. Barnabas, taken during the war (or shortly before), is complex.
On one level, the image of Mr. Barnabas is propaganda, showcasing the success of the German educational mission and the loyalty of the Askari.
The composition of the photograph of Mr. Barnabas is choreographed, with Barnabas at the center, radiating knowledge.
The photograph of Mr. Barnabas also documents the reality of African literacy and the formation of a new social class—the Askari intelligentsia—who would play a crucial role in the colony’s future.
The photograph of Mr. Barnabas demonstrates that the newspaper was not just a tool of German power, but a medium through which Africans were negotiating their own modernity.
Perhaps Walther Dobbertin’s most enduring contribution is his landscape photography of the Usambara Mountains.
The Usambara Mountains, with their cool climate and lush rainforests, were the center of European settlement.

Walther Dobbertin traveled extensively in the Usambara Mountains, hauling his heavy camera gear up steep trails to capture panoramic vistas of the Lua Valley, the mission station at Gare, and the precipitous drops of the escarpment.
Walther Dobbertin's images of the Usambara Mountains are technically superb.
Walther Dobbertin's glass plates captured an immense amount of detail, from the species of trees in the forest canopy to the erosion patterns on the cultivated slopes.

Aesthetically, Walther Dobbertin's Usambara landscapes framed the region as a "German Heimat" in Africa—a landscape that, with its orderly fields and misty peaks, could remind a settler of the Black Forest or the Harz.
Walther Dobbertin operated in an era of transition for photographic technology.
Walther Dobbertin primarily used large-format cameras with glass plates (likely dry gelatin plates).
Walther Dobbertin's glass plates, often 13x18cm or larger, offered resolution that rivals modern high-end digital cameras.
Walther Dobbertin's glass plates were heavy, fragile, and slow.
To achieve his shots, Walther Dobbertin was as much an expedition leader as a photographer.
Walther Dobbertin required porters to carry his equipment, tripods, and darkroom supplies.
In the field, Walther Dobbertin had to judge exposure by eye, as light meters were primitive.
The distinct aesthetic of Walther Dobbertin's photos—deep depth of field, sharp focus throughout—was a result of using small apertures (high f-stop), which in turn required long exposure times.
The long exposure times necessitated by Walther Dobbertin's photographic techniques required the absolute stillness of his subjects, contributing to the stiff, posed look of his portraits.
Walther Dobbertin's landscapes benefited from the clarity provided by his photographic techniques.

When World War I erupted in August 1914, German East Africa found itself surrounded by hostile colonial powers: British Kenya to the north, the Belgian Congo to the west, and Portuguese Mozambique to the south.
The commander of the Schutztruppe, Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, adopted a strategy of aggressive defense, aiming to tie down as many Allied troops as possible in a protracted guerrilla war.
Upon mobilization for World War I, the German male population was conscripted.
Walther Dobbertin joined the Schutztruppe, not merely as a soldier but in a capacity that utilized his professional skills.
While the Western Front had official propaganda companies (Bild- und Filmamt), the East African theater was isolated.
Walther Dobbertin became, by default and by talent, the primary—and arguably the only—photographer systematically documenting the German campaign in East Africa.
Walther Dobbertin’s wartime archive is a unique historical document.
Walther Dobbertin's wartime archive captures the transformation of the colonial police force into a battle-hardened army.
Walther Dobbertin documented the aftermath of the Battle of Tanga (November 1914), a decisive German victory against a poorly led British amphibious landing.
Walther Dobbertin chronicled the logistical miracle of the SMS Königsberg.
After the German cruiser SMS Königsberg was trapped and sunk in the Rufiji Delta, its ten 10.5cm naval guns were salvaged.
Walther Dobbertin photographed the massive 10.5cm naval guns from the SMS Königsberg being mounted on improvised gun carriages and dragged through the bush by teams of hundreds of porters.
Walther Dobbertin's images of the SMS Königsberg guns serve as a testament to the ingenuity and improvisation that characterized the German war effort.
Walther Dobbertin's most politically potent images from the war period are those of the Askari.
Walther Dobbertin photographed the Askari on the march, cleaning their Mauser rifles, and manning machine gun nests.
Walther Dobbertin's photos of the Askari emphasize discipline, order, and an apparent camaraderie between white officers and black soldiers.
One famous series by Walther Dobbertin shows "Camel-mounted Schutztruppe" on patrol near the Kilimanjaro/Longido area, illustrating the diverse and adaptive nature of the force.
Another image by Walther Dobbertin depicts a machine gun team in action, the tension of combat frozen on the glass plate.

Walther Dobbertin's images of the Askari would later be stripped of their context and used to propagate the myth that the Askari fought out of sheer devotion to the Kaiser, ignoring the complex motivations of pay, status, and coercion that actually drove recruitment.
Snippet 1 mentions that Walther Dobbertin also shot scenes for a documentary film during the early stages of World War I.
Cinema was in its infancy, and a war documentary from Africa would have been a sensation.
Walther Dobbertin's documentary film footage from the early stages of World War I has been lost to history, likely destroyed during the retreat or confiscated.
Only Walther Dobbertin's still images remain to reconstruct the visual narrative he intended to create with his lost documentary film footage.
By 1916, the sheer numerical superiority of the Allied forces (British, South African, Indian, Belgian) began to tell.
The Schutztruppe was forced to abandon the Northern Railway and retreat south into the Rufiji wilderness.
It was during the retreat of the Schutztruppe that Walther Dobbertin was captured by the British.
Walther Dobbertin spent the remainder of World War I, roughly 1916 to 1919, as a Prisoner of War (POW).
German POWs in East Africa were typically held in camps in Egypt, India, or localized holding areas in Dar es Salaam before repatriation.
A significant historical puzzle arises regarding photographs in the Dobbertin archive dated to 1918 and early 1919.
Snippet 4 highlights a specific image showing General von Lettow-Vorbeck and a British staff officer, dated March 1918 (or possibly post-surrender in 1919).
If Walther Dobbertin was a prisoner in 1916, it raises the question of how he could have taken a photo of Lettow-Vorbeck in the field in 1918.
One theory for the 1918 photo controversy is attribution error, where the photo was taken by a British photographer or another German soldier and later acquired by Dobbertin.

Another theory for the 1918 photo controversy is post-surrender photography, where Dobbertin, if held in Dar es Salaam, was released or allowed to photograph the arrival of the undefeated General in early 1919 before their mutual repatriation.
Following the Armistice in November 1918, Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered at Abercorn and marched his troops to Dar es Salaam.
A third theory for the 1918 photo controversy is dating error, where the dates in the archives may simply be incorrect.
The consensus among historians tends toward attribution error or the acquisition of negatives from other sources regarding the 1918 photo controversy.
The Bundesarchiv collection, "Nachlass Walther Dobbertin," contains materials Walther Dobbertin owned, not necessarily only those he took, though he is the primary author of the vast majority.
While Walther Dobbertin languished in a POW camp, his wife, Alwine Dobbertin, performed a feat of archival rescue.
As the British administration took over and German property was seized, Alwine Dobbertin managed to smuggle the heavy, fragile glass plates out of the country.
The logistics of Alwine Dobbertin smuggling glass plates out of the country are remarkable, as glass plates are dense and breakable.

Smuggling hundreds of glass plates past military censors and onto a repatriation ship suggests a high degree of determination and perhaps the assistance of sympathetic officials or hidden compartments.
Without Alwine Dobbertin’s actions, the visual history of German East Africa would be significantly poorer, and Walther’s post-war career would have been impossible.
In 1920, the Dobbertins were repatriated to Germany.
The Dobbertins arrived in a Germany that had changed unrecognizably: the Kaiser had abdicated, the economy was in ruins, and the Treaty of Versailles had stripped Germany of all its colonies.
Walther Dobbertin settled in Northern Germany, in the quiet heathland south of Hamburg.
Walther Dobbertin moved to Wiedenhof, a district of Jesteburg, and established a business in the nearby towns of Buchholz and Harburg.
Walther Dobbertin opened a bookshop (Buchhandlung) and a publishing house (Kunstverlag).
Walther Dobbertin's primary asset for his business was the crates of glass plates Alwine had saved.
In a Germany humiliated by defeat, there was a potent market for nostalgia—for images of a time when Germany was a world power with a tropical empire.
The Weimar Republic was rife with "colonial revisionism."
The political movement of colonial revisionism sought to refute the "Colonial Guilt Lie" (Kolonialschuldlüge)—the Allied justification that Germany was too brutal to rule colonies.
Colonial revisionists argued that German rule had been benevolent, scientific, and progressive.
Walther Dobbertin’s photos were the perfect evidence for the colonial revisionist argument.
Walther Dobbertin began publishing postcards and books that emphasized "German Work."
Walther Dobbertin's 1920 book Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika was an explicit visual rebuttal to Versailles.
Walther Dobbertin's book Von deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika showed bridges, schools, and hospitals, arguing visually that Germany had developed the territory for the benefit of all.
The culmination of Walther Dobbertin's revisionist phase was the publication of Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks (Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers) in 1932.
Walther Dobbertin self-published Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks from his home in Wiedenhof.
Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks contained 120 high-quality copperplate engravings of Walther Dobbertin's wartime photos.
Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks was not just a history; it was a hagiography.
Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks presented the East African campaign as a clean, heroic struggle, contrasting sharply with the industrialized slaughter of the Western Front.
The captions in Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks, written in a nationalist register, celebrated the "fidelity" of the Askari and the genius of Lettow-Vorbeck.
Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks was instrumental in solidifying the legend of Lettow-Vorbeck, who was himself a prominent right-wing political figure in the Weimar era.
Walther Dobbertin’s images provided the visual iconography for General Lettow-Vorbeck’s memoirs, creating a feedback loop of myth-making that portrayed the colonial army as "undefeated in the field."
When the Nazis seized power in 1933, the colonial revisionist movement was absorbed into the state’s expansionist ideology.
Walther Dobbertin, already a nationalist and a veteran, aligned himself with the new Nazi order.
Walther Dobbertin joined the Sturmabteilung (SA), the "Brownshirts," which was the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party.
Walther Dobbertin's membership in the SA indicates that he was not merely a passive fellow traveler but an active participant in the party apparatus.
Walther Dobbertin became a district leader (Kreisleiter or similar local functionary) for the Reichskolonialbund (RKB), the Reich Colonial League.

The Reichskolonialbund (RKB), led by Franz Ritter von Epp, was tasked with keeping the "colonial thought" alive in the German population, preparing them for the eventual reclamation of the overseas territories.
Under the aegis of the RKB, Walther Dobbertin’s archive was mobilized for mass propaganda.
Walther Dobbertin's photos were converted into lantern slides for lectures given in schools and community halls across Germany.
Walther Dobbertin's photos were used in major colonial exhibitions, such as the ones in Dresden (1939) and Vienna (1940).
In the Nazi context, Walther Dobbertin’s images of orderly plantations and loyal African subordinates took on a darker ideological hue.
Walther Dobbertin's images were used to validate the Nazi theories of racial hierarchy and the concept of Lebensraum (living space).
The "German Work" in Africa was presented as a precursor to the German colonization of Eastern Europe—a demonstration of the German ability to order and exploit "primitive" lands.
Walther Dobbertin continued to profit from the use of his archive in Nazi propaganda.
In 1933, Walther Dobbertin's photos illustrated Alfred Funke’s novel Schwarz-Weiß-Rot über Ostafrika, a piece of colonial fiction that indoctrinated the youth with the romance of the lost empire.
With the collapse of the Third Reich in 1945, the colonial dream was finally extinguished.
British troops occupied Northern Germany in 1945.
Walther Dobbertin, as a known member of the SA and a Nazi functionary, fell under the scrutiny of the denazification process.
The British authorities revoked Walther Dobbertin's business license in 1945, effectively banning him from publishing or selling books.
Revoking business licenses was a standard measure against those deemed to have actively supported the Nazi regime.
Like many of his generation, Walther Dobbertin was eventually rehabilitated.
By the late 1940s or early 1950s, Walther Dobbertin was back in business, though the exact date of the restoration of his license is unclear.
Walther Dobbertin spent the 1950s running his bookshop in Wiedenhof.
The clamor for colonies had died down, replaced by the Cold War and the distinct challenges of the Wirtschaftswunder.
Walther Dobbertin remained a local figure, the keeper of a specific, fading memory.
Walther Dobbertin never returned to Africa during the interwar or Nazi periods.
It was only in 1960/1961 that Walther Dobbertin planned a return trip to Tanzania, which was then on the verge of independence from British rule.
Walther Dobbertin intended to revisit the landscapes he had photographed half a century earlier.
Walther Dobbertin died on January 12, 1961, in Jesteburg-Wiedenhof, shortly before his scheduled departure.
Walther Dobbertin was 78 years old when he died.
Following Walther Dobbertin's death, his widow sold the collection to the German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) in Koblenz.
The "Nachlass Walther Dobbertin" (BILD 105) comprises approximately 3,000 images.
The acquisition of Walther Dobbertin's collection by the Bundesarchiv transformed it from a private commercial asset into public property, accessible to researchers.
Walther Dobbertin's archive includes images from German South West Africa (Namibia) and Cameroon, though East Africa remains the core.
In recent years, the most innovative use of Walther Dobbertin’s work has come from the field of environmental history.
Professor Chris Conte of Utah State University initiated the Usambara Knowledge Project, which uses Dobbertin’s landscapes as scientific data points.
Professor Conte and his team located the exact spots where Walther Dobbertin stood in roughly 1910.
Professor Conte and his team took new photographs to create a "then and now" comparison with Walther Dobbertin's images.
The findings from the Usambara Knowledge Project were revelatory.

Contrary to narratives of pure destruction, some areas showed forest regeneration, while others showed the replacement of indigenous cloud forest with exotic species introduced by the Germans (eucalyptus, wattle).
Walther Dobbertin's photos revealed the transition from the German plantation economy to the peasant agriculture of modern Tanzania.
The expansion of settlements into previously uninhabited slopes was visibly measurable using Walther Dobbertin's photos.

Walther Dobbertin’s technical obsession with sharpness and depth of field meant that individual trees and erosion gullies from 1910 could be identified, making his "colonial gaze" an inadvertent tool for modern conservation science.
Scholars like Heike I. Schmidt and others have used Walther Dobbertin's archive to critique the visual culture of colonialism.
Scholars argue that Walther Dobbertin’s photos did not just record reality; they created it.
By photographing the "native" in specific ways—as a servant, a warrior, or a type—Walther Dobbertin helped to construct the racial categories that underpinned colonial rule.
Walther Dobbertin's archive is also seen as a site of "visual repatriation."

Digitalization projects are increasingly making Walther Dobbertin's images available to Tanzanians, allowing descendants of the Askari and the porters to see their ancestors, not as colonial subjects, but as historical actors in their own right.
Walther Dobbertin was a man of his time, and his life followed the tragic arc of German nationalism in the 20th century.
Walther Dobbertin was a pioneer who helped build a colony, a soldier who fought to defend it, a propagandist who tried to resurrect it, and finally, a relic of a vanished world.
Walther Dobbertin's intentions were undoubtedly colonialist; he sought to glorify "German Work" and German dominance.
The quality and comprehensiveness of Walther Dobbertin's work have allowed it to escape his ideological grasp.

Today, Walther Dobbertin's photographs serve purposes he could never have imagined: they are evidence for the prosecution in the court of history regarding colonial exploitation, but they are also precious baselines for the ecological salvation of the Usambara Mountains.
Walther Dobbertin left behind more than just propaganda; he left a high-resolution memory of a world that changed the course of African and European history forever.

# Conditions Governing Use 

The Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa is the physical property of the 

Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Literary rights, including copyright, belong 

to the authors or their legal heirs and assigns. For further information, consult the appropriate curator. 

# Preferred Citation 

Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa. General Collection, Beinecke Rare 

Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. 

# Processing Information 

Collections are processed to a variety of levels, depending on the work necessary to make them usable, 

their perceived research value, the availability of sta, competing priorities, and whether or not further 

accruals are expected. The library attempts to provide a basic level of preservation and access for all 

collections, and does more extensive processing of higher priority collections as time and resources 

permit. 

This collection received a basic level of processing, including rehousing and minimal organization. 

This finding aid may be updated periodically to account for new acquisitions to the collection or 

revisions in arrangement and description. 

Information included in the Content Description note and Collection Contents section is drawn 

from information supplied with the collection and from an initial survey of the contents. Portions 

of description for this collection have been directly repurposed from description supplied with the 

collection upon its receipt. Folder titles appearing in the contents list below are often based on those 

provided by the creator or previous custodian. Titles have not been verified against the contents of the 

folders in all cases. Otherwise, folder titles are supplied by sta during initial processing. 

Upon receipt, the collection was titled "From Cape to Cairo collection," as assigned by Humphrey 

Winterton and Maggs Brothers. The collection title was changed during processing in 2020. 

# Scope and Contents 

This collection consists of photograph albums, loose photographs, memorabilia and published material 

that document a European colonialist perspective of Africa and Egypt, and document both African peoples 

and European colonizers. Locations depicted in the photographs include Cameroon, Dar es Salaam, Egypt, 

Kenya, Namibia, Sudan, Tanga, Zambia, other regions throughout Africa, as well as some in Europe. 

Identified photographers in this collection include Alfredo Augusto Freire de Andrade, Walther Dobbertin, 

Paul Karl Lieberenz, and Carl von Vincenti. The bulk of photographs in the collection are created by 

unidentified photographers.

Organized into seven series: I. Southern Africa, 1890 - 1929. II. Central Africa, circa 1918. III. East Africa, 1887 -

2005. IV. West Africa, 1880 - 1934. V. North Africa, 1904 - 1935. VI. Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910 - 1920. VII. 

Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910 - 1933.

b.  30  Egypt and Sudan photograph albums by Henry Maitland Wilson 

Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland Wilson, G.C.B., G.B.E., D.S.O. (1881-1964) 

attended Eton and Sandhurst before being commissioned into the Rifle Brigade 

as a 2nd Lieutenant in May 1900. Nicknamed "Jumbo", Wilson's military career 

included service in the Boer War and World War I, before attaining the rank of 

General and overseeing operations in the Middle East and Mediterranean. 

Between 1939 and 1944, he held various commands in North Africa and the Middle 

East when he succeeded General Eisenhower as Supreme Allied Commander of 

the Mediterranean Theatre. He was a confidant of Winston Churchil and was 

made Field Marshall in 1944. Three years later he became Chief of the British Joint 

Sta Mission in Washington D.C. where his friendship with Eisenhower prospered 

(to the extent that Eisenhower provided an introduction to Wilson's volume of 

wartime memoirs). In 1944 he became Baron Wilson of Libya and of Stowlangtoft. 

These photograph albums document a hunting trip in Sudan and Egypt and 

contain 163 photographs with captions. One album is signed "HM Wilson Rifle 

Brigade" on the front pastedown. 

These albums record a hunting trip made with Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland 

Wilson and fellow soldiers along the White Nile. Included are photographs of 

African communities, including the Shilluk people, the Baggara, the Nuer people, 

and the Dinka people. Other images depict big game hunting, fellow travellers, as 

well as markets, the boats on which they sailed, and life along the shores of the 

Nile.

and Ismailia in the early months of the war. There is a selection of images 

featuring artillery, inspection lines, the Australian camp at Giza, US ships at 

Alexandria, and bridge building. 

Other images depict individuals traveling throughout Egypt, a picnic on the Nile 

on Easter Sunday, 1915, Egyptian fruit sellers, fishermen, and coast guards. The 

final photographs are of a military hospital in Reading. The newspaper clippings all 

relate to the Dardanelles campaign, particularly Gallipoli. 

circa 1910s 

Page  15  of  20 Series V: North Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  32  Egypt World War I photograph album 

This album contains 400 photographs documenting British troops in Egypt during 

World War I. The photographer was based in the British camp at Beni Salama, 

which is situated about 60 kilometers north west of Cairo on the western edge 

of the Nile delta. Photographs depict Egyptian people, firing practice, camp 

accommodations in the desert (tents, latrines), troops riding horseback and 

camels, meals, feluccas on the Nile, the sphinx and pyramids at Giza, street scenes 

in Cairo, the Muhammad Ali Mosque, and the ancient monuments at Luxor. The 

group portraits are of the Ocers of the Woolwich Sub-Command London AA 

Defences. 

1916 

b.  33  Egypt, France, Italy, and Sudan photograph album 

This album of Egypt, Sudan, Italy, Sicily and France contains 202 photographs. 

The annotations are detailed and provide information on the various ports and 

cities encountered. The bulk of this annotated album comprises photographs 

taken in Egypt and in Sudan as the photographer appears to have travelled down 

the Nile on the ship Straithaird. African communities represented include the 

Dinka people, the Shilluk people, the Nuer people, and the Bari people. Towns or 

ports documented include Taormina, Port Said, Port Sudan, Melut, Malakal, Sambe, 

Malek and Khartoum, before the photographer ventures back to northern Italy 

and the south of France, ending finally in Provence. 

1933–1935 

Page  16  of  20 Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910–1920 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs documenting locations including Algeria, Egypt, 

Ghana, Kenya, and other locations in Africa. Images depict big game hunting, European colonialists, African 

colonial subjects, and architecture. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  34–35  Africa and Egypt photograph albums 

These albums document a trip from Southern Africa to Cairo and contains 576 

photographs. The opening images in the first album are of Zambezi River at 

Victoria Falls. Images in the albums depict a big game hunting safari undertaken 

on both sides of the river in both Northern and Southern Rhodesia (present day 

Zambia and Zimbabwe). Images include the hunting party which consisted of 

the European colonialists and African people, as well as the game that was killed, 

including elephant, bualo, a lion and lioness, zebra, warthog, wild boar, hyena, gnu 

and antelope. Included is a series of photographs of young rhinos on a farm being 

hand-reared and bottle-fed, as well as young bualo being loaded into a crate and 

the onto a rear of a truck. 

Photographs in the second album depicts African people and European 

colonialists on big game hunts. Other images document an Ocean voyage, and 

scenes depicting the Sphinx and the Great Pyramid of Giza. The end of the album 

depictcts large European-style houses, ostriches and pelicans in cages. The 

remainder of the album include more images of Cairo and Giza, as well as images 

of individuals. 

circa 1920 

b.  31  Algeria, Ghana, and Kenya photographs 

This group of five photographs includes one of Algeria, inscribed, "Alger: La 

Kasbah: Rue de la Mer Rouge." Two other photographs are inscribed with "Accra" 

on the verso and depict the docks of Ghana. Two other photographs depict groups 

of Bantu peoples of Western Kenya. 

circa 1910 

Page  17  of  20 Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910–1933 

This series contains primarily printed material created by European colonialists about Africa. Included 

are volumes of photographic reproductions, published material, and a photograph album. The material 

documents how a colonial perspective of Africa was produced and distributed to a European audience. 

Material is arranged chronologically. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  36–37  Die Deutschen Kolonien 

Two volume sets of bound photographic reproductions, with additional mounted 

photographic reproductions. The first set is divided into the following volumes: 

I. Togo, II. Kamerun, III. Deutsch-Südwestafrika. The second set contains the 

following volumes: I. Deutsch-Ost-Afrika, II. Kaiser-Wilhelmsland und die Inselwelt 

im Stillen Ozean, III. Samoa, IV. Kiautschou. 

All the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Printing was done by the Institute for Colour Photography, Carl Weller, Berlin. 

circa 1910 

b.  31  Deutschlands Kolonien by Willy Scheele 

First edition by Weller and Hüttich, Berlin. 1912. 63 of the 80 images and 124 pages 

of the text are devoted to the German colonies in Africa including Togo, Kamerun, 

Deutsch-Südwestafrika, and Deutsch-Ostafrika. 

1912 

b.  31  Farbfotografien aus den Deutschen Kolonien by Willy Scheel 

2 Folders 

48 color oset lithography reproductions with printed captions. Foreword by 

Dr. Scheel, including the narrative, "Overview of the German Colonies." The 48 

illustrations have been selected from the 80 which are included in Dr. Scheel's 

book. Though primarily devoted to German colonies in Africa, this set of images 

provides photographs of Togo, Cameroon, German Southwest Africa, German 

East Africa, New Guinea, Caroline Islands, the Bismarck Archipelago, Samoa, and 

Kiatschou Bay. 

All of the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Publication is by Carl Weller of the Institute for Colour Photography, Berlin. 

1913 

b.  38  Das Kolonial Wirtschaftliche Komitee Berlin Kolonial Ausstellung By Paul 

Lieberenz 

The Colonial Economic Development Committee of Berlin was founded in the late 

nineteenth century for the purpose of finding and identifying tropical plants and 

agricultural crops which could be commercially exploited. It mounted numerous 

expeditions for this purpose, frequently to remote areas not previously visited 

by Europeans. Its work was greatly hampered after Germany's loss of its colonies 

during and after the First World War. In the 1920s Germany was in political 

and economic turmoil and, by the end of 1930, parliamentary democracy had 

eectively given way to an increasingly authoritarian regime with the National 

Socialists gaining ground. Against this background, the politicians were looking 

for ways to restore Germany's influence abroad, including the former colonies. 

Original commemorative photographic album produced by Paul Lieberenz for 

the German Colonial Exhibition held in Berlin in May 1933. The album contains 

14 photographs, including a printed introductory essay by the Committee's 

Chairman, Dr. h. c. A. Drehn. 

There is documentation of the racist practice of including live humans in 

anthropological displays, featuring people from Africa who were brought over to 

Berlin to be used in the exhibition. 

1933

Other images include general views of the exhibition, including a thatched stand 

of the "Frauenbund der Deutschen Kolonialgesellschaft," a display for "Frauverein

Gebeite, a display of Deutsch Ost Afrika which features agricultural produce,

comprising mainly of photographs and displays in glass cases, and the display of 

Kamerun and Togo featuring carved wooden objects such as stools, woven straw 

hats, fans, and textiles.

2.title: Walther Dobbertin
2.content:
aus Wikipedia, der freien Enzyklopädie

**Walther Alexander Dobbertin** (* [28. August](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/28._August "28. August")[1882](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1882 "1882") in [Berlin](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin")[[1]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-1); † [12. Januar](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/12._Januar "12. Januar")[1961](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961 "1961") in [Jesteburg-Wiedenhof](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesteburg "Jesteburg")[[2]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:1-2)) war ein deutscher Fotograf und Verleger, der hauptsächlich in der ehemaligen Kolonie [Deutsch-Ostafrika](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Ostafrika "Deutsch-Ostafrika"), im Gebiet des heutigen [Tansania](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tansania "Tansania"), tätig war. Sein fotografisches Werk, das aus Hunderten von Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen besteht, bietet eine umfassende Darstellung der politischen, sozialen, wirtschaftlichen und militärischen Aspekte der Kolonie. Seine Motive reichen von Landschaften und Wildtieren bis hin zu Porträts von Einheimischen und deutschen Siedlern. Vor allem dokumentierte er die Aktivitäten der deutschen [Schutztruppe](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutztruppe "Schutztruppe") und in den Anfangsjahren des [Ersten Weltkriegs in Ostafrika](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erster_Weltkrieg_in_Ostafrika "Erster Weltkrieg in Ostafrika").

Dobbertin wurde als Kind einer Berliner Handwerkerfamilie geboren. Seine Vorfahren stammten aus [Mecklenburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecklenburg "Mecklenburg"), wo sich das [Kloster Dobbertin](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloster_Dobbertin "Kloster Dobbertin") befindet. In [Rostock](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostock "Rostock") durchlief er eine Fotografenlehre und besuchte Malkurse.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)

1903 wanderte Walther Dobbertin nach Deutsch-Ostafrika (DOA) aus. Nach seiner Ankunft arbeitete er für einige Jahre im [Fotostudio](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fotostudio "Fotostudio") von [Carl Vincenti](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Vincenti "Carl Vincenti") in Daressalam.[[4]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-4) 1907 kam es zwischen Vincenti und Dobbertin zu einem heftigen Streit, der vor Gericht ausgetragen wurde. Vincenti warf Dobbertin vor, fotografisches Material gestohlen bzw. unterschlagen zu haben.[[5]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:3-5) Dobbertin wurde daraufhin zu einer Gefängnisstrafe von drei Tagen und Übernahme der Gerichtskosten verurteilt.[[6]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-6)

Nachdem Dobbertin sich anschließend selbstständig gemacht hatte, gründete er in Daressalam, [Tanga](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanga_(Tansania) "Tanga (Tansania)") und [Moshi](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshi_(Stadt) "Moshi (Stadt)") Buch- und Kunsthandlungen. Er entwickelte sich in den folgenden Jahren zu einem der bedeutendsten Fotografen Deutsch-Ostafrikas. Nach dem Ausbruch des [Ersten Weltkrieges](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erster_Weltkrieg "Erster Weltkrieg") war er der einzige Fotograf, der die Geschehnisse in der umkämpften Kolonie auf deutscher Seite dokumentierte.[[7]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-7)

1916 geriet Dobbertin als Mitglied der deutschen [Schutztruppe](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutztruppe_f%C3%BCr_Deutsch-Ostafrika "Schutztruppe für Deutsch-Ostafrika") in englische Gefangenschaft. Bei Kriegsende wurden die Deutschen aus Ostafrika ausgewiesen und enteignet. Der Frau Dobbertins, Alwine, gelang es aber, die fotografischen Platten ihres Mannes außer Landes zu schmuggeln. Nach seiner Entlassung aus der Gefangenschaft kehrte Dobbertin nach Deutschland zurück und zog nach Wiedenhof, heute ein Ortsteil von [Jesteburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesteburg "Jesteburg"), südlich von [Hamburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). Dort eröffnete er erneut eine Buchhandlung.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)

1932 veröffentlichte Dobbertin unter dem Titel _Die Soldaten [Lettow-Vorbecks](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul\_von\_Lettow-Vorbeck "Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck")_. _Ein Buch vom deutschen Wehrwillen und deutscher Waffenehre_ im Selbstverlag eine Sammlung verherrlichender Soldatenporträts aus der deutsch-ostafrikanischen Kolonialzeit. Neben 120 [Kupfertiefdrucken](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiefdruckverfahren "Tiefdruckverfahren") seiner Aufnahmen in DOA enthält die englische Übersetzung von 2005 ein Nachwort über Dobbertins Leben.[[8]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-8) In der [Zeit des Nationalsozialismus](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeit_des_Nationalsozialismus "Zeit des Nationalsozialismus") war Dobbertin Mitglied der [SA](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturmabteilung "Sturmabteilung") und [Kreisleiter](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kreisleiter "Kreisleiter") des [Reichskolonialbundes](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichskolonialbund "Reichskolonialbund"). Wegen dieser Tätigkeiten wurde ihm 1945 von der britischen Besatzungsbehörde die Lizenz zum Betrieb seines Geschäftes entzogen. Nachdem er die Erlaubnis zurückerhalten hatte, betrieb er die Buchhandlung bis 1960. Kurz vor einer geplanten Reise nach Afrika, der ersten nach seiner Rückkehr im Jahre 1920, starb Dobbertin am 12. Januar 1961.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)[[2]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:1-2)

Nach seinem Tod verkaufte Dobbertins Witwe seine persönlichen Dokumente, Fotoplatten und Fotos an das [Bundesarchiv](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesarchiv_(Deutschland) "Bundesarchiv (Deutschland)"), wo sie archiviert wurden.[[9]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-9)

[![Image 1: People working on a railroad](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_Sisalernte.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_Sisalernte.jpg)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datei:Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958,_Deutsch-Ostafrika,_Sisalernte.jpg)

Sisalernte in DOA

Dobbertins Fotografien des kolonialen Lebens in Deutsch-Ostafrika umfassen Hunderte von Bildern politischer, sozialer, wirtschaftlicher und militärischer Ereignisse, darunter Aufnahmen von Großwildjagd und Wildtieren, Naturlandschaften und dem Bau von Eisenbahnen. Seine Fotografien von Afrikanern zeigen die einheimische Bevölkerung und ihr Alltagsleben unter der Kolonialherrschaft. Dazu gehören Bilder von Askari-Soldaten der deutschen Schutztruppe ebenso wie anderer Bewohner der Kolonie, wie beispielsweise Inder und [Swahilis](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_(Gesellschaft) "Swahili (Gesellschaft)"). Andere Bilder zeigen das Leben auf dem Land, darunter Afrikaner, die auf einer [Sisal](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisalfaser "Sisalfaser")plantage arbeiten oder Kinder am Ufer eines Flusses, die Einbäume zu Wasser lassen und fischen.[[10]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-10)

**Eigene Bücher und Fotoillustrationen**

*   _Landschaftsbilder_ _aus Deutsch-Ost-Afrika_. Daressalaam: Kunstverlag Walther Dobbertin, 1910. OCLC number 838068870.
*   _Bilder_ _aus dem Negerleben_. Daressalaam: Kunstverlag Walther Dobbertin, 1910. OCLC number 838068839.

*   _Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks_. Ein Buch vom deutschen Wehrwillen und deutscher Waffenehre. 120 künstlerische Kupfertiefdrucke nach Aufnahmen aus dem Weltkriege in Deutsch-Ostafrika / hrsg. von Walther Dobbertin, Wiedenhof-Buchholz. 1932 (Nachdruck Jerxheim: Jericksen Historischer Verlag, 2019, [ISBN 978-3-96569-013-4](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spezial:ISBN-Suche/9783965690134)). Englische Ausgabe: _Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers. A Book of German Fighting Spirit and Military Honor._ Battery Press, Rockford, Ill., Nashville, 2005, [ISBN 978-0-89839-3-408](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spezial:ISBN-Suche/9780898393408).
*   [Hermann Löns](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_L%C3%B6ns "Hermann Löns"), _Grün ist die Heide_. Eine Auswahl von 25 der besten Novellen, Jagd-, Tier- und Naturschilderungen. Mit 112 Lichtbildern aus dem gleichnamigen Film und nach Aufnahmen von Walther Dobbertin, Hannover 1932.
*   [Alfred Funke](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Funke "Alfred Funke"), _Schwarz-Weiß-Rot über Ostafrika_. Roman. Mit 126 Lichtbildern von Walther Dobbertin, Hannover 1933.

*   [![Image 3: Schutztruppe mit Revolverkanone](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0149%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_An_der_Revolverkanone.jpg/330px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0149%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_An_der_Revolverkanone.jpg)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datei:Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0149,_Deutsch-Ostafrika,_An_der_Revolverkanone.jpg "Schutztruppe mit Revolverkanone")

Schutztruppe mit Revolverkanone

*   [![Image 4: Bogenschützen in Ruanda-Urundi](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0157%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2CWarundi-Bogensch%C3%BCtzen.jpg/500px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0157%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2CWarundi-Bogensch%C3%BCtzen.jpg)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datei:Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0157,_Deutsch-Ostafrika,Warundi-Bogensch%C3%BCtzen.jpg "Bogenschützen in Ruanda-Urundi")

Bogenschützen in [Ruanda-Urundi](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruanda-Urundi "Ruanda-Urundi")
